*Question from gemini: How do systemic vascular and metabolic risk indicators—such as history of coronary heart disease, diabetes, and blood pressure—correlate with neurological markers of brain damage, specifically brain tissue atrophy and brain infarct volume? (delete later)*

Load libraries

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

Load the clean and augmented data

```{r}
clean_data <- read_tsv(file = "../data/03_dat_aug.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Create new subset `cor_data` with selected variables associated with cardiovascular and brain health

```{r}
cor_data <- clean_data |> 
  select("atrophy", #brain 
         "numinf",  #brain 
         "stroke",  #brain 
         "volinf",  #brain
         "whgrd",   #brain
         "dsst",    #brain
         "chf",     #cd ~ cardiovascular
         "chd",     #cd
         "sbp",     #cd
         "ldl",     #cd
         "diabetes",#cd
         "plt",     #cd
         "aai")     #cd
```

Investigate the subset

```{r}
cor_data |> 
  str() 
```

Prepare the dataset for correlation analysis: The variables `stroke` and `chd` are ordinal, including 3 categories (0,1,2). We split the initial variables into 2 new ones:

-stroke -\> stroke_tia (tia: transient ischemic attack), stroke_event

-chd -\> chd-angina, chd_mi (mi: myocardial infarction) (abbreviations from rigr package documentation)

*(use of AI assistance)*

```{r}
cor_data <- cor_data |>
  # create the dummy variables
  mutate(stroke_tia = as.numeric(stroke == 1),
         stroke_event = as.numeric(stroke == 2),
         chd_angina = as.numeric(chd == 1),
         chd_mi = as.numeric(chd == 2)) |>
  # remove the initial variables from the subset
  select(-stroke,
         -chd)
```

Check normality of numeric (continuous, discrete) variables to choose the correlation method.

```{r}
shapiro.test(cor_data$numinf)
shapiro.test(cor_data$volinf)
shapiro.test(cor_data$dsst)
shapiro.test(cor_data$sbp)
shapiro.test(cor_data$ldl)
shapiro.test(cor_data$plt)
shapiro.test(cor_data$aai)
```

The variables in the subset are classified as binary, ordinal, discrete or continuous and the majority of the numeric ones are not normally distributed (p-value\<0.05), for this reason we choose the Spearman correlation method.

Study the correlation between the variables associated with brain and cardiovascular health

```{r}
# create correlation matrix
 cardio_vars<- cor_data |> 
   select(dsst, # continuous
         atrophy, # ordinal 
         whgrd, # ordinal
         numinf, # discrete
         volinf, # continuous
         stroke_tia, # binary
         stroke_event) # binary 
 brain_vars <- cor_data |> 
  select(sbp, # continuous
         ldl, # continuous
         aai, # continuous
         chf, # binary
         diabetes, # binary
         chd_angina,# binary
         chd_mi, # binary
         plt) # discrete
 cor_matrix <- round(cor(cardio_vars,
                         brain_vars,
                         method = "spearman"), 5)
```

Investigate correlation matrix

```{r}
cor_matrix |> 
 range()
```

Tidy the data frame before visualization

```{r}
cor_tbl <- cor_matrix |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "brain") |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -brain,
               names_to = "cardiovascular",
               values_to = "correlation")
```

Create a heatmap to visualize the results from the correlation matrix

```{r}
cor_plot <- cor_tbl |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = brain,
             y = cardiovascular,
             fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "darkolivegreen",
                       mid = "white",
                       high = "darkmagenta",
                       midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-0.35,0.35)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation between brain and cardiovascular variables",
       x = "Brain variables",
       y = "Cardiovascular variables",
       fill = "Spearman correlation",
       caption = "Note: Color scale limited to [-0.35, 0.35] to improve visual contrast.")+
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
cor_plot

ggsave("../results/08_analysis_4/correlation_plot.png",
       cor_plot,
       width = 8,
       height = 11,
       dpi = 300)
```

The heatmap shows that the correlations between the two sets of variables are weak, as their values have a range of -0.16570 - 0.20605 and the correlation is stronger when the value is closer to +/- 1.

(I will change it)

The strongest positive correlation in this analysis, is between the `dsst` variable (Digit Symbol Substitution Test score) and the `aai` (Ankle Brachial Index). More specifically, Ankle Brachial Index reflects overall vascular health and blood flow, while the Digit Symbol Substitution score is a neurophychological test used to assess cognitive performance. Therefore, a higher aai (within the normal range) indicates better circulation which helps maintain healthy blood flow to the brain and supports faster cognitive processing on the dsst. This connection between blood flow and brain function explains why the two variables show a possible correlation, although other demographical factors might influence the result. In contrast, `plt` and `ldl` show no correlation with any of the brain variables.

```{r}
#delete
p0 <- cor.test(cor_data$dsst, cor_data$aai, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
p0
```

Next, we will focus on other variables that show weak positive correlations in the heatmap, to test their p-values and check whether these correlations are statistically reliable.

Variables: `sbp`, `chd_mi`, `atrophy`, `volinf`

```{r}
# correlation test to check p-values
# exact = FALSE : calculate an approximate p-value when the values of variables are identical
p1 <- cor.test(cor_data$sbp, cor_data$atrophy, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$p.value
p2 <- cor.test(cor_data$sbp, cor_data$volinf, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$p.value
p3 <- cor.test(cor_data$chd_mi, cor_data$atrophy, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$p.value
p4 <- cor.test(cor_data$chd_mi, cor_data$volinf, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$p.value

p.adjust(c(p1,p2,p3,p4))
```

The associations between `sbp` and `chd_mi` with `volinf` are statistically significant as their p-values are below 0.05. These results make biological sense, as higher blood pressure can damage the blood vessels of the brain. Furthermore, myocardial infarction increases the risk of clots which can lead to brain infracts. However, the correlations are weak and the data are observational, so they show an association but not causation.
